en: The *Guanla Jing* (Sutra on the Anniversary Offering after Parinirvāṇa), translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Zhu Fahu of the Yuezhi Kingdom during the Western Jin Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, together with...
The great assembly of bhikṣus, together with the devas and humans, were gathered and seated, listening as the Sūtra was being preached.
Ānanda came forward, knelt with his hands joined in *añjali*, and addressed the Buddha, saying: “O God among Gods!
I wish to ask a question; I pray that the Buddha will explain it!

After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, what should the fourfold assembly of disciples—bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās—do on the eighth day of the fourth month and the fifteenth day of the seventh month during the Kaḷyāṇī festival?
The Buddha said to Ānanda:

“As for the Buddha Varṣākāra, he was one who delivered those who possessed merit and aspiration; each person reduced their wealth and treasures, relinquished what they cherished, and used it to seek the merit of liberation from the world.
They provided lamps for the monastery, burned incense, and used the funds to create scriptures and images.”
If one makes offerings to a teacher and gives them to the poor, one may arrange a vegetarian feast.

One must not permit [the teacher] to borrow [the items], for if they are not returned, this constitutes a betrayal of the Buddha in the present life. Since this is an act committed by both mind and speech, one shall incur the sin of lying.

Why is this? Because when one offers a bowl to the Buddha and pays homage, personally bathing the Buddha with five kinds of scented water while the teacher recites the *dakṣiṇā* and offers prayers of blessing—at that very moment, devas, nāgas, and spirits all clearly witness and know it. If a person takes wealth from the five families and even encroaches upon their wives' and children's portions to seek merit and blessings, yet fails to contribute [to the offering], they shall incur five offenses and enter the three evil realms.

What are these five? First, one's wealth and possessions diminish daily; second, one is prone to forgetfulness and loss; third, whatever business one undertakes for a livelihood yields no profit; fourth, upon entering the Tai Shan Hell, one undergoes interrogation and punishment, the agony of which is difficult to describe; fifth, in a future life, one may be reborn as a slave, or as an ox, horse, mule, donkey, or camel, or even as a pig or sheep.
These are the five.
Furthermore, there are three further evils:

first, entering among the *pūtani* to become a hungry ghost; second, entering among birds and beasts to become an animal; and third, within the *niraya*, one shall undergo the eighteen hells, where the offenses are beyond counting.

"On the fifteenth day of the seventh month, one personally honors the parents of seven generations and five kinds of relatives who may have fallen into the evil realms and suffer intense affliction; by virtue of the merit made through prostrating to the Buddha, one seeks to bring them liberation from sorrow and suffering—this is called *guǎnlà* (the ritual of pouring [fragrant water])."
“The Buddha is the King of the heavens above and the worlds below within the triple realm; he does not consume the offerings of worldly people.
All such things should be distributed among the Sangha and must not be taken up alone, for this constitutes a grave offense.
If there is no Sangha to distribute them, one should give them to the poor, the solitary, and the weak and aged; this plants roots of goodness.”

Upon hearing this sutra, the disciples rejoiced, prostrated before the Buddha, and departed. [From] the *Guanla jing* (The Sutra on the Offering of the Anniversary of Parinirvāṇa), following the Parinirvāṇa.
